concept.name: Bull pennant
concept.definition: A short-term continuation pattern consisting of a sharp advance (the flagpole) followed by a brief consolidation bounded by converging trend lines forming a small symmetrical triangle (the pennant), typically lasting one to three weeks. It is read as a pause of market indecision within an uptrend, with continuation expected on a breakout above the pennant's upper line on increased volume. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: After a sudden rally the market catches its breath in ever-tighter swings; the triangle-shaped breather ends when buyers overwhelm sellers again and price shoots out of the apex.
concept.mechanics: Require a strong pole on large volume, then a converging triangular consolidation on weakening volume, and finally a breakout with a large volume increase. Traders commonly enter just above the pennant's upper trend line, place the stop at the pennant's lowest point, and set a target by adding the flagpole's height to the breakout price. Confirmation with indicators such as RSI is standard practice.
concept.formula: Price target = B + P, where B = breakout price above the pennant's upper trend line and P = flagpole height (pole top minus pole base).
concept.failure_modes: Entering before the breakout (anticipating) is the classic failure — consolidation can resolve downward through the lower line. Low participation (weak volume) during the pennant, or external news shocks, frequently break the expected continuation.
concept.misconceptions: That pennants and flags are the same pattern — pennants have converging lines (a small symmetrical triangle), flags have parallel lines; duration also differs (pennants typically one to three weeks, longer contractions are triangles).
concept.example: A stock rallies from $5 to $10, consolidates in a tightening triangle around $8.50–$9.00, then breaks out at $9.00 on a volume surge; the flagpole method projects a target near $14.
